Recommendations / next steps:

3) We’ll schedule a short engineering deep-dive next week to discuss stop-sequence semantics and retry/fallback behavior.

Thanks Marissa — that all sounds good. A couple quick notes from our engineering side after the demo:

- We observed partial output coherence sometimes — e.g., the stream would emit a truncated sentence that looked fine until the next token arrived and then it changed meaning. This is a UX problem for clinicians.
- Stop sequences: our UI expects a deterministic marker ("<STOP_CLINICAL>") emitted reliably to close the suggestion. We saw a few responses where the model emitted an ellipsis or newline instead and the client didn't close the suggestion.
- Latency: target is <150ms per streaming chunk on average; bursts up to 250ms acceptable.

Can you include in the eval notes: per-token latency distribution and frequency of non-deterministic stop tokens? Also any guidance on prompt engineering to reduce mid-stream flips would be helpful.

Sam

Subject: Re: Demo recap & next steps — model fit & streaming UX

Hi Sam — digging in from the engineering side. High-level notes below; I’ll attach a quick report and a short runbook.

Model-fit recommendations:
- Candidate models: rw-13b-quant (best latency/quality tradeoff for streaming), rw-7b-qat (faster, slightly lower coherence), rw-13b-int8 (highest fidelity but slower in our hosted config).
- Quantization: for your throughput/latency targets I recommend the 13b-quant profile (mixed int8 kernels + KV cache optimizations).

Streaming UX guidance (partial output / stop sequences):
- Partial-token flips: usually caused by lookahead differences between model logits sampling and client render logic. Mitigations: 1) buffer N=2 tokens on the client before committing a sentence; 2) use a punctuation-aware flush policy so the UI waits for a punctuation token or explicit <STOP_CLINICAL>.
- Stop sequence reliability: enforce a strong stop token via both prompt engineering and model-side filter. Example prompt suffix we use: "
<STOP_CLINICAL>
" (explicit token with rare probability elsewhere). We can also configure server-side post-filtering to treat <STOP_CLINICAL> as terminal even if probabilities are low.

Metrics we’ll produce in the eval:
- Per-token latency p50/p90/p99 (streaming emission times)
- Stop-token omission rate (how often the stream ends without emitting the explicit token)
- Coherence flip rate (tokens that change semantic meaning within a 5-token window)

I’ve attached a short eval-quickreport.pdf with preliminary numbers on a 100-sample pass. Full 500-sample to follow.

Links: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/acme-health/2026-06 (benchmark dashboard)
HubSpot: https://hubspot.com/deal/ACME-2026-EXP-42

Appreciate the detail Jordan. A couple follow-ups:

- Buffering: buffering 2 tokens before commit could help but adds UI latency. Do you have data on user-perceived latency impact vs reduction in flips?
- Stop token: will the server-side post-filtering always force the token even if the model assigns it low prob? How does that affect natural completions (we worry about truncated clinical phrases)?
- Quality regression: we rolled a new prompt variant last week and saw a ~6% drop in clinical-accuracy in our internal checks. If we use model pinning/rollbacks, what's the fastest path to rollback in Redwood Dedicated?

If you can include the buffer impact numbers in the full eval that would be helpful. Also happy to schedule the engineering deep-dive — Tue/Wed next week work for us.

Sam
